title: Gus Lamont's grandmother reveals why she believes he was abducted
text:
By MAISY RAE - NEWS REPORTER and KARLEIGH SMITH - SENIOR REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  10:39 AEST, 22 September 2026   |  Updated:  11:04 AEST, 22 September 2026

The grandmother of missing child Gus Lamont has revealed she believes he was abducted from near her South Australian sheep station because 'nothing else makes sense'.

Four-year-old Gus was last seen playing near the remote homestead, 40km south of Yunta, on September 27. Despite extensive land and air searches, the little boy has never been seen since.

In February, police said they believed someone known to Gus may have killed him, deliberately or accidentally, before he was reported missing.

Police said the suspect lived at Oak Park Station, 300km north of Adelaide, and was known to the child.

They also said the person was not his mother, Jessica Murray, or his father, Joshua Lamont, who lived at Belalie North, a two-hour drive away.

On Monday, Gus's grandmother, Josie Murray, revealed she now believes Gus was abducted by a stranger.

'I think he has to have been taken. Nothing else makes sense,' she told 7News.

She said she still wanted 'to know the answer [to] what happened to him' before directing TV cameras to the area where Gus was playing on the afternoon he disappeared.

'It brings me to tears that he's not here... Just down here. And then that was the last he was seen, and after that he just disappeared,' she said.

Four-year-old Gus Lamont was last seen playing near his grandparents' remote homestead in South Australia on September 27

His grandmother, Josie Murray, believes he was abducted by a stranger

Police have searched Oak Park Station 11 times since Gus vanished last September

Gus's grandparents, Shannon and Josie Murray, both live at and own the station.

Josie later confirmed that police had told her she is the main suspect in the case. She has consistently maintained her innocence.

No charges have been laid and no arrests have been made.

Josie's comments come weeks after South Australian police refused to confirm whether they still have a person of interest in Gus' disappearance.

They also refused to confirm whether they have identified any other suspects.

At the time, Josie's lawyer, Andrew Ey, told the Daily Mail: 'My client has always remained steadfast in her denial' of being involved in Gus's disappearance.'

An extensive land, air and dam search by police, the army, the SES, an Aboriginal tracker and local volunteers, which ran for several weeks, has failed to find any sign of the boy.

Initially, police fiercely defended the family's request for privacy as they navigated Gus's mysterious disappearance and fading hopes that he would be found, alive or dead.

But in January, the working relationship between Josie and Shannon and Task Force Horizon investigators suddenly soured, with police later confirming the case had turned into a major crime investigation.
